opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the underappreciated implications of the timelines question. When people's timelines were very short, say a few years, there was a natural pull toward interventions that could pay off almost immediately: working inside the leading labs, voluntary commitments, technical work you could ship quickly. The things that take a long time, like building public understanding, passing durable legislation, or creating international institutions, looked almost irrelevant, because they might not mature before the critical period was already over.

If timelines are longer, say we're looking at a decade or more before truly transformative systems, a much wider range of options opens up. Take democratic politics. Getting an issue onto the public agenda, having it debated, building cross-party coalitions, drafting careful laws, and then implementing and enforcing them is a slow process. It often takes many years. With longer timelines, that becomes a real option rather than a fantasy.

The same goes for international coordination. Treaties, verification regimes, and something like an international agency for advanced AI all need a lot of groundwork: trust between states, technical methods for monitoring compute or training runs, and diplomatic relationships that let you negotiate. You can't build those in eighteen months. In ten or fifteen years, you might.

There's also a talent and institutional-capacity dimension. Governments currently have very few people who deeply understand these systems. Longer timelines mean it's worth investing in training a generation of civil servants, regulators, and legislative staff who can actually engage with the technical details. That's a slow investment, but it compounds.

I'd add a caveat, though. Longer timelines in expectation don't mean we can relax. There's still meaningful probability on shorter scenarios, so we want a portfolio: some things that help if transformative AI arrives soon, and some slower, more foundational work that pays off if we have more time. What I worry about is the community having over-indexed on the short-timeline strategies, so the slower, more legitimate, more democratic routes have been relatively neglected. If we do have more time, those could be where a lot of the value lies, partly because solutions built through broad public buy-in tend to be more robust and harder to unwind than deals struck quietly among a handful of companies.

r001.rationale: The response says strategies focused on leading labs may be overemphasized, but does not say they would become misguided if companies stopped being the leading AI actors.

r002.rationale: It mentions international treaties generally, but not that seeing extraordinarily capable AI could increase appetite for a China–United States treaty.

r003.rationale: It does not connect AI-related economic hardship to opposition to AI becoming electorally successful.

r004.rationale: It discusses regulation and slower democratic processes, but does not say politicians could view slowing AI progress as a regulatory benefit rather than a cost.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most underrated aspects of the whole timelines debate. People tend to treat timelines as if the only thing they affect is how urgent things are, how fast we need to run. But actually, timelines also change what kind of race it is. They change the terrain, not just the clock.

If you think transformative AI is two or three years away, then the only interventions that really matter are the ones that can be executed by the people who already hold power. That means the existing frontier labs, the existing executives, the current administrations in the US and China, maybe a handful of regulators who are already in post. You're essentially locked into working with the cast of characters as they stand today, and you're mostly limited to things like voluntary commitments, executive orders, lab-internal policies, perhaps some export controls. Those are real levers, but they're a narrow set, and many of them are fragile. An executive order can be rescinded by the next administration in an afternoon.

If instead you think we're looking at something more like ten or fifteen or twenty years, the picture opens up enormously. For one thing, legislation becomes possible in a serious way. Proper statutory frameworks, with licensing regimes, liability rules, mandatory safety testing, that sort of thing. Those take years to design, years to pass, and years to actually bed in, so they're basically off the table on very short timelines but very much on the table with longer ones.

Then there's the international dimension. Treaties are slow. The nuclear arms control agreements took decades to negotiate and build the verification machinery for. If you think there's a decade or more, then something like an international agreement on compute thresholds, or inspection regimes for large training runs, or a shared body that monitors frontier development, stops being a fantasy and becomes a legitimate project to start on now. You might not get there, but you can at least make an honest attempt.

Longer timelines also change who can be in the room. On short timelines, you're stuck with whoever happens to have influence right now. On longer timelines, you can actually build a field of people with the right expertise and get them into government, into regulatory agencies, into the labs, into the international bodies. You can shift public opinion in a durable way rather than relying on a single moment of panic. And I think democratic legitimacy actually matters here. Decisions made in a rush by a tiny group of people, even well-meaning ones, are much harder to sustain than ones that have gone through a proper public process.

There's one more thing I'd add, which is that longer timelines make it possible to be more ambitious about the goal itself. If you have two years, you're mostly trying to avoid the worst outcomes with whatever tools are to hand. If you have twenty, you can ask bigger questions, like what sort of governance structures we actually want for a technology this consequential, and whether it should be developed in quite the way it's being developed now at all. You get to make choices about the shape of the thing, not just react to it.

So I'd say that the key thing is not to let the short-timeline framing crowd out the slower, more robust interventions. Even if you put substantial probability on things happening quickly, there's still significant probability on it taking longer, and the interventions that pay off in those longer worlds are often the ones that are most durable. I'd want a portfolio that covers both, rather than betting everything on the sprint.

r002.rationale: It proposes possible international agreements and monitoring regimes, but does not connect witnessing extraordinarily capable AI to increased appetite for a China–United States treaty.

r003.rationale: It mentions shifting public opinion, but not widespread AI-related economic hardship or opposition to AI becoming electorally successful.

r004.rationale: It describes regulation and other durable interventions, but does not say politicians could view slowing AI progress as a benefit of regulation rather than a cost.

astra-6.text:
I think longer timelines could make quite a big difference, because they give us time to build institutions rather than having to work almost entirely through the institutions we already have. If you think the most consequential developments are coming in two or three years, then you’re looking at what existing governments and companies can do very quickly. There may be useful interventions there, but the range is quite constrained.

If we have a couple of decades, then you can start thinking about international agreements, new regulatory bodies, and building the expertise within governments to make those bodies effective. You can also pursue research whose political payoff takes time: developing ways to verify compliance with an agreement, for example. An agreement that sounds desirable in principle may become much more feasible if countries have a credible way to check that others are following it.

Of course, having more time doesn’t mean that those things will happen automatically. It means we have an opportunity to lay the groundwork. And because we’re uncertain about timelines, I’d want a portfolio: some work that can help on very short timelines, alongside work that could put us in a much better position if we have longer.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss AI-related economic hardship or its potential electoral effects.

r004.rationale: It describes possible regulation and agreements, but does not say politicians could view slowing AI progress as a benefit of regulation rather than a cost.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think longer timelines could open up a much wider range of political interventions. If you think that very powerful AI is coming in the next few years, you’re largely constrained to working with the institutions and political circumstances that we already have. You can try to get governments to take the issue seriously, build up technical expertise, and introduce some safeguards, but there’s only so much institutional change you can achieve in that time.

If we have several decades, then you can start thinking about building new institutions, negotiating international agreements, and developing forms of cooperation that would currently seem politically unrealistic. Something being infeasible today is much less decisive if you have twenty or thirty years to work towards it.

Of course, that time doesn’t automatically produce better governance. You would need to use it. And because we’re uncertain about timelines, I think we should pursue things that could help in the short term while also laying the foundations for more ambitious cooperation if we have longer.
